claim: Correlations between the activities of peripheral afferents mediate a phase invariant representation of natural communication stimuli in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus.
source: Previously we reported that correlations between the activities of peripheral afferents mediate a phase invariant representation of natural communication stimuli that is refined across successive processing stages thereby leading to perception and behavior in the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus (Metzen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Metzen et al., 2016).

claim: Increasing background frequency led to phase locking in peripheral afferents.
source: We found that increasing background frequency led to phase locking, which decreased both detectability and phase invariant coding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing background frequency decreased both detectability and phase invariant coding.
source: We found that increasing background frequency led to phase locking, which decreased both detectability and phase invariant coding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D, 2E, and 3C, 3D.

claim: Correlated afferent activity was a much better predictor of behavior than single neuron activity in terms of both invariance and detectability.
source: Correlated afferent activity was a much better predictor of behavior as assessed from both invariance and detectability than single neuron activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing neural and behavioral responses shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Natural electrocommunication signals (chirps) preferentially occur on top of low frequency sinusoidal backgrounds.
source: Thus, our results provide not only further evidence that correlated activity likely determines perception of natural communication signals, but also a novel explanation as to why these preferentially occur on top of low frequency as well as low-intensity sinusoidal backgrounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental results and established knowledge about chirp occurrence patterns.

claim: Chirps can occur at any phase of the beat with uniform probability.
source: Behavioral data shows that chirps can occur at any phase of the beat with uniform probability (Walz et al., 2013; Aumentado-Armstrong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: A chirp with given duration and frequency increase can give rise to very different patterns of stimulation depending on the beat phase at which it occurs.
source: Thus, a chirp with given duration and frequency increase can give rise to very different patterns of stimulation depending on the beat phase at which it occurs (Benda et al., 2005; Marsat et al., 2009; Walz et al., 2013, 2014; Metzen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and is also demonstrated in Figure 1E.

claim: Single neuron spiking activity of peripheral electrosensory afferents did not provide a phase invariant representation.
source: We previously found that the single neuron spiking activity of peripheral electrosensory afferents did not provide a phase invariant representation as these faithfully encoded the different stimulus waveforms resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases of the beat.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to previous findings and is confirmed by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Correlations between afferent spike trains systematically increased in response to the chirp irrespective of beat phase.
source: However, when instead considering population activity, we found that correlations between afferent spike trains systematically increased in response to the chirp irrespective of beat phase, thereby providing a phase invariant representation.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to previous findings and is demonstrated in Figure 2C for low beat frequencies.

claim: Pyramidal cells within the electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL) showed 'locally' phase invariant responses.
source: Recordings from pyramidal cells within the electrosensory lateral line lobe (ELL) receiving synaptic input from multiple peripheral afferents showed that their responses were 'locally' phase invariant (i.e. they gave similar responses only to stimulus waveforms resulting from a given chirp occurring at some but not all beat phases).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to previous experimental recordings.

claim: Neurons within the midbrain Torus semicircularis (TS) showed a 'globally' phase invariant representation.
source: Recordings from neurons within the midbrain Torus semicircularis (TS) revealed the emergence of a more 'globally' phase invariant representation as these responded to the different stimulus waveforms resulting from the same chirp occurring at different beat phases through similar increases in firing rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to previous experimental recordings.

claim: Weakly electric fish gave similar behavioral responses to patterns of stimulation resulting from the same chirp occurring at different beat phases.
source: Finally, we showed that weakly electric fish gave similar behavioral responses to patterns of stimulation resulting from the same chirp occurring at different beat phases, suggesting that the globally phase invariant representation of chirps in midbrain is decoded and further refined downstream (Metzen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to previous behavioral experiments.

claim: Chirps are emitted on top of beats with frequencies spanning a wide range.
source: However, behavioral data shows that chirps are emitted on top of beats with frequencies spanning a wide range (Zakon et al., 2002), which gives rise to further heterogeneities in the resulting stimulus waveforms (Zupanc and Maler, 1993; Hupé et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Chirp stimulus waveforms are more similar to the background itself for higher beat frequencies.
source: It is important to note that chirp stimulus waveforms are more similar to the background itself for higher beat frequencies (Figure 1E, compare columns).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1E.

claim: The 'frequency contrast' between the beat and the chirp is lower for higher beat frequencies, making differentiating chirp signals from the background beat more difficult.
source: This is because the 'frequency contrast' between the beat and the chirp is then lower, which makes differentiating chirp signals from the background beat more difficult (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F demonstrating decreased detectability.

claim: The stimulus waveforms resulting from the same chirp occurring at different beat phases remain equally different from one another irrespective of background beat frequency.
source: Despite this decrease in detectability, it is important to notice that the stimulus waveforms resulting from the same chirp occurring at different beat phases remain equally different from one another irrespective of background beat frequency, as quantified by the average distance between all possible combinations of chirp signals at a given beat frequency (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Single afferent responses consisted of patterns of increases and decreases in firing activity that strongly depended on the stimulus waveform that was presented.
source: Single afferent responses consisted of patterns of increases and decreases in firing activity that strongly depended on the stimulus waveform that was presented (Figure 2B, blue curves; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, blue raster plots).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For all beat frequencies, single neuron activity strongly varied depending on where the chirp occurred within the beat cycle.
source: For all beat frequencies, single neuron activity strongly varied depending on where the chirp occurred within the beat cycle (Figure 2C, top, blue curves).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The duration of the single neuron response to chirps decreased as a function of increasing background beat frequency.
source: Interestingly, we found that the duration of the single neuron response to chirps decreased as a function of increasing background beat frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, blue) despite the fact that the actual chirp duration (i.e. the time interval during which there is an increase in EOD frequency, see Figure 1D) is constant by construction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Single afferent activity showed low invariance values for all background beat frequencies.
source: We found low values for all background beat frequencies (Figure 2D, blue curve). This indicates that the distance between responses was always more or less equal to the distance between the corresponding stimulus waveforms.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Single afferents displayed phase locking to the beat for higher background beat frequencies.
source: It is important to note that single afferents displayed phase locking (Keener et al., 1981; Trussell, 1999) to the beat for higher background beat frequencies as action potentials reliably occurred only during a restricted range of phases during the beat cycle (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B, and is consistent with cited literature on phase locking.

claim: Phase locking in afferents results from the fact that afferents display high-pass filtering properties.
source: Such phase locking results from the fact that afferents display high-pass filtering properties (Bastian, 1981; Xu et al., 1996; Chacron et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing afferent filtering properties.

claim: Background beats with higher frequencies elicit greater modulations in firing rate around the baseline value, thereby increasing the probability of rectification.
source: As such, background beats with higher frequencies will elicit greater modulations in firing rate around the baseline (i.e. in the absence of stimulation) value, thereby increasing the probability of rectification (i.e. cessation of firing).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the high-pass filtering properties of afferents and is supported by experimental observations in Figure 2B.

claim: The range of stimulus phases during which the firing rate is null increases with beat frequency.
source: Indeed, the range of stimulus phases during which the firing rate is null increases with beat frequency (Figure 2B, compare blue traces).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Periods of complete cessation of firing decrease the distance between responses to chirps occurring at different beat phases, thereby slightly increasing the invariance score for higher (>32 Hz) beat frequencies.
source: It is these periods during which there is complete cessation of firing that decrease the distance between responses to chirps occurring at different beat phases, thereby slightly increasing the invariance score for higher (>32 Hz) beat frequencies (Figure 2D, blue).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and is supported by Figure 2D showing increased invariance at higher frequencies.

claim: Single afferent responses to the chirp are as variable as the responses to the beat itself for all beat frequencies.
source: When instead considering detectability, we found that single afferent responses to the chirp are as variable as the responses to the beat itself for all beat frequencies (Figure 2E, blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Detectability of chirps as quantified from single afferent activity was low for all beat frequencies.
source: Consequently, detectability of chirps as quantified from single afferent activity was low for all beat frequencies (Figure 2E, blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The duration of the response to a chirp using correlated activity decreased as a function of increasing background beat frequency.
source: We found that the duration of the response to a chirp using correlated activity decreased as a function of increasing background beat frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, purple) and therefore used time windows whose duration matched those observed experimentally for correlated activity to quantify invariance using the same measure as done previously (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: For low (<16 Hz) background beat frequencies, afferent spiking activity was synchronized either through large increases in firing rate or cessation of firing after chirp onset but not during the beat.
source: For low (<16 Hz) background beat frequencies, we found that afferent spiking activity was synchronized either through large increases in firing rate or cessation of firing after chirp onset but not during the beat (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was an increase in correlation after chirp onset irrespective of the beat phase the chirp occurred at for low background beat frequencies.
source: Thus, there was an increase in correlation after chirp onset irrespective of the beat phase the chirp occurred at for low background beat frequencies (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, purple traces), consistent with our previous results.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: For higher background beat frequencies (>32 Hz), afferents displayed strong phase locking, causing increased synchrony through cessation of firing during the beat itself at the population level.
source: For higher background beat frequencies (>32 Hz), afferent activity was still synchronized either through large increases in firing rate or cessation of firing after chirp onset. However, afferents also displayed strong phase locking as mentioned above, thereby causing increased synchrony through cessation of firing during the beat itself at the population level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Afferent activities became more correlated with one another only for some portions of the beat cycle as the beat frequency is increased.
source: Thus, afferent activities became more correlated with one another only for some portions of the beat cycle (i.e. those for which there is cessation of firing) as the beat frequency is increased (Figure 2B, purple traces).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Correlated activity no longer provided a phase invariant representation of chirp stimuli for higher beat frequencies.
source: First, we found that correlated activity no longer provided a phase invariant representation of chirp stimuli for higher beat frequencies (Figure 2C,D, purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Invariance values strongly decreased as background beat frequency increased.
source: Consequently, we found that invariance values strongly decreased as background beat frequency increased (Figure 2D, purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Phase locking in single afferent responses is strongly detrimental to phase invariant coding by correlated activity.
source: We therefor conclude that phase locking in single afferent responses is strongly detrimental to phase invariant coding by correlated activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing decreased invariance with increased phase locking.

claim: Correlated activity during the beat became more similar to those elicited by the chirp as background beat frequency is increased, thereby decreasing detectability by correlated activity.
source: Specifically, correlated activity during the beat became more similar to those elicited by the chirp as background beat frequency is increased (Figure 2B, purple), thereby decreasing detectability by correlated activity (Figure 2E, purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2E.

claim: Behavioral responses to chirps for higher background beat frequencies were no longer invariant.
source: Confirming hypothesis 1), we found that echo responses were more dissimilar to one another for high beat frequencies (Figure 3B). Consequently, there was a strong decrease in behavioral invariance at background beat frequencies >32 Hz (Figure 3C, brown).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: There was a good match between invariance scores obtained from correlated activity and behavior.
source: Further evidence strongly suggesting that correlated afferent activity is decoded by downstream neurons comes from a good match between invariance scores obtained from correlated activity and behavior (Figure 3C, compare brown and purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of neural and behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a poor match between invariance as computed by single afferent activity and behavior.
source: In contrast, there was a poor match between invariance as computed by single afferent activity and behavior (Figure 3C, compare brown and blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of neural and behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a strong decrease in echo response rate as a function of increasing background beat frequency.
source: We found that there was a strong decrease in echo response rate as a function of increasing background beat frequency (Figure 3D, brown), thereby confirming hypothesis 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a strong match between echo response rate and detectability as computed from correlated but not single afferent activity.
source: Importantly, there was a strong match between echo response rate and detectability as computed from correlated but not single afferent activity (Figure 3D, compare brown, purple and blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of neural and behavioral data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The characteristics (frequency excursion and duration) of the chirps elicited for different background beat frequencies were not significantly different from one another.
source: We found that the characteristics (i.e. frequency excursion and duration) of the chirps elicited for different background beat frequencies were not significantly different from one another (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Small chirp stimuli occur preferentially on top of low frequency beat backgrounds.
source: Specifically, it is well known that the small chirp stimuli considered here occur preferentially on top of low frequency beat backgrounds (Bastian et al., 2001; Engler and Zupanc, 2001; Zakon et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: The decreased signal detectability was due to the greater tendency of peripheral afferents to display phase locking to higher background beat frequencies.
source: We have also shown that the decreased signal detectability was due to the greater tendency of peripheral afferents to display phase locking to higher background beat frequencies, which is a direct consequence of their high-pass frequency tuning characteristics (Bastian, 1981; Xu et al., 1996; Chacron et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results and is supported by citations to previous studies on afferent tuning properties.

claim: Phase locking causes increased correlations among afferents during some portions of the background beat for which both afferents do not fire action potentials.
source: Such phase locking causes increased correlations among afferents during some portions of the background beat for which both afferents do not fire action potentials.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing phase locking and correlated activity patterns.

claim: Greater variability in correlation throughout the beat cycle decreases signal detectability.
source: This greater variability in correlation throughout the beat cycle then decreases signal detectability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Small chirps occur more rarely on top of beats with higher frequencies because such chirps cannot be encoded and perceived irrespective of the beat phase at which they occur.
source: Thus, our results support the hypothesis that small chirps occur more rarely on top of beats with higher frequencies because such chirps cannot be encoded and perceived irrespective of the beat phase at which they occur.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Small chirps are preferentially elicited when both fish are located farther away from one another.
source: Previous studies have also shown that small chirps are preferentially elicited when both fish are located farther away from one another (Hupé and Lewis, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous behavioral study.

claim: Small chirps seldom occur when both fish are in close vicinity (e.g. biting distance).
source: Indeed, such stimuli seldom occur when both fish are in close vicinity (e.g. biting distance).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from behavioral observations.

claim: The background beat contrast increases as distance between both fish decreases.
source: In this context, it is important to realize that the background beat contrast (i.e., how strong the beat amplitude is relative to each animal's unmodulated electric field amplitude) increases as distance between both fish decreases (Yu et al., 2012; Fotowat et al., 2013; Metzen and Chacron, 2014) and there is a lot of interest in understanding how the time-varying beat amplitude is encoded by electrosensory neurons (Savard et al., 2011; McGillivray et al., 2012; Metzen and Chacron, 2015; Metzen et al., 2015; Huang and Chacron, 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Martinez et al., 2016; Zhang and Chacron, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Peripheral afferents will display phase locking in response to low beat frequencies when the beat amplitude is high enough, such as when both animals are right next to one another but not when located further apart.
source: In particular, previous studies have found that peripheral afferents will display phase locking in response to low beat frequencies when the beat amplitude is high enough, such as when both animals are right next to one another but not when located further apart (Nelson et al., 1997; Kreiman et al., 2000; Metzen and Chacron, 2014, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The beat amplitudes used in this study are in agreement with those experienced when both fish are located further apart.
source: Thus, while the beat amplitudes used in this study are in agreement with those experienced when both fish are located further apart (Metzen and Chacron, 2014) such that peripheral afferents did not display significant phase locking, it is clear that these same afferents will do so at low-frequency beat backgrounds at higher amplitudes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and describes the experimental conditions used.

claim: Phase locking at low-frequency beat backgrounds at higher amplitudes will be detrimental on signal detectability and phase invariant coding.
source: We predict that such phase locking will be detrimental not only on signal detectability but also on phase invariant coding for the same reasons that we found for higher background beat frequencies.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The segregation of behaviorally relevant signals from a varying background is an important task that many sensory systems must solve.
source: This is because the segregation of behaviorally relevant signals from a varying background is an important task that many sensory systems must solve (auditory system: [Brumm and Todt, 2002; Lohr et al., 2003; Woolley et al., 2005; Ronacher et al., 2008; Berti, 2013]; visual system: [Born et al., 2000; Olveczky et al., 2003]; electrosensory system: [Zakon et al., 2002; Vonderschen and Chacron, 2009]).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations across different sensory systems.

claim: Correlations between the activities of neighboring neurons are observed ubiquitously in the brain.
source: Moreover, correlations between the activities of neighboring neurons are observed ubiquitously in the brain (Averbeck et al., 2006) and are dynamically regulated by several factors such as attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009), behavioral state (Vaadia et al., 1995) and stimulus statistics (Chacron and Bastian, 2008; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2012; Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2013; Simmonds and Chacron, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurons will display phase locking in response to sinusoidal stimulation, thereby enhancing their response selectivity.
source: Moreover, it is well known that neurons will display phase locking in response to sinusoidal stimulation (Johnson, 1980), thereby enhancing their response selectivity (Lee et al., 2005; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Feature invariance has been demonstrated across sensory systems (visual, auditory, olfactory).
source: Finally, we note that feature invariance has been demonstrated across sensory systems (visual: [Zoccolan et al., 2007]; auditory: [Bendor and Wang, 2005]; olfactory: [Martelli et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in different sensory modalities.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by McGill University's animal care committee under protocol number 5285.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by McGill University's animal care committee under protocol number 5285.
evidence: The claim is a statement of fact about ethical approval.

claim: Apteronotus leptorhynchus specimens were acquired from tropical fish suppliers and acclimated to laboratory conditions according to published guidelines.
source: Apteronotus leptorhynchus specimens were acquired from tropical fish suppliers and acclimated to laboratory conditions according to published guidelines (Hitschfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and is supported by a citation to published guidelines.

claim: Recordings were made from 116 peripheral receptor afferents.
source: We recorded from single peripheral receptor afferents (N = 116) (Figure 2A) in response to different patterns of sensory input resulting from the same chirp stimulus occurring at different phases of a background beat with varying frequency.
evidence: The claim describes the sample size of the experimental data.

claim: Behavioral responses were recorded from 33 fish with a total of 3467 chirps.
source: To test these hypotheses, we recorded behavioral responses to patterns of stimulation resulting from the same chirp occurring at different phases within a beat cycle with different frequencies (N = 33 fish; n = 3467 chirps) (Figure 3A) using a previously established behavioral paradigm that measures echo chirp responses (Zupanc et al., 2006; Hupé et al., 2008; Metzen et al., 2016) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the sample size of the behavioral experiments.

claim: Small chirps are characterized as a short duration (10–20 ms) increase in EOD frequency of about 60–150 Hz.
source: Small chirps are characterized as a short duration (10–20 ms) increase in EOD frequency of about 60–150 Hz and can thus be considered 'high-frequency transients' (Zupanc and Maler, 1993; Engler and Zupanc, 2001); see also Walz et al. (2013) for review).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing small chirps.

claim: The stimulus intensity used ranged between 0.14 mV/cm and 0.61 mV/cm (average: 0.34 ± 0.15 mV/cm).
source: The stimulus intensity was set such that electrosensory afferents did not display non-linear responses such as rectification for beat frequencies up to 10 Hz and ranged between 0.14 mV/cm and 0.61 mV/cm (average: 0.34 ± 0.15 mV/cm).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental parameters used.

claim: The stimulus intensity was held constant for all stimuli used to elicit responses from a given afferent.
source: Importantly, the stimulus intensity was held constant for all stimuli used to elicit responses from a given afferent.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The stimulus intensities used for behavioral experiments were similar to those used for recording from afferents.
source: The stimulus intensities used for behavioral experiments were similar to those used for recording from afferents.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.
